sections.h2: What changes when a Lakewood owner sells a rental or a worn house?
sections.html:
Lakewood adds a city step for landlords: an owner who sells a non-owner-occupied rental needs a certificate of code compliance, which depends on a point of sale inspection. The certificate rule applies to non-owner occupied rentals. For an owner living in the house, the choice runs among an agent, a by owner sale and a cash buyer.

  • Agent listing: reaches the most buyers for a tidy, updated house, with weeks set aside for inspections and financing.
  • Sale by owner: you set the price, run tours and complete the disclosure paperwork.
  • Cash buyer: takes the house in whatever shape it is in, which suits a double with deferred repairs, a rental with a pending inspection, or a house left by an estate.

Because only 44.4 percent of Lakewood homes are owner occupied, buyers and sellers here see rentals, doubles and small apartment buildings often. Knowing the city's rental rules early keeps a closing date from sliding.

sections.h2: Why does Lakewood have so many older houses?
sections.html:
Lakewood grew as one of Cleveland's streetcar suburbs. The area was surveyed as Rockport Township in 1806 and incorporated as a village in 1889, named for its place on Lake Erie. Streetcars reached it on Detroit Avenue in 1893, Clifton Boulevard in 1903 and Madison Avenue in 1916, and the population jumped from 3,355 in 1900 to 70,509 by 1930. That is why the nickname is City of Homes.

Neighborhoods carry distinct building stock. Birdtown, an eight street district on the southeast side with bird names, was built in the 1890s for National Carbon Company workers and joined the National Register in 2006. Clifton Park in the northwest corner holds Victorian mansions near the lake, and Victorian Village on the east end housed company executives. Rockport Square added roughly 200 condos and lofts from 2004 along Detroit Avenue, and the Gold Coast high rises sit on the lakefront.

Lakewood is dense, with 9,190 people per square mile on only 5.54 square miles of land. That density shows up in the small lots and close neighbors a buyer will see on every block.

sections.h2: How does Lakewood's population profile differ from its neighbors?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau puts Lakewood at 49,027 people on July 1, 2025, a 3.7 percent decline from the 2020 base of 50,930. The table shows other traits that set Lakewood apart.

sections.h2: How do Lakewood schools, roads and the lakefront shape a sale?
sections.html:
Public schools belong to the Lakewood City School District: Lakewood High School, Garfield and Harding middle schools and seven elementary schools. The district rebuilt or renovated its buildings in a program finished in 2017, the first major school construction program since 1920. Private options include Lakewood Catholic Academy and St. Edward High School.

  • Highways: Interstate 90 runs along the south side with ramps at West 117th Street, Bunts Road, Warren Road and McKinley Road.
  • Transit: Greater Cleveland RTA buses cover Clifton Boulevard, Detroit Avenue, Madison Avenue, Warren Road and West 117th Street, and Red Line rapid stations sit just across the Cleveland border.
  • Lakefront and parks: Lakewood Park is one of the largest lakefront parks in Ohio, and the Rocky River Reservation of the Cleveland Metroparks forms part of the western edge.

A Cleveland Clinic family health center opened in 2018 across the street from the former Lakewood Hospital site. Downtown Cleveland is about 6 miles to the east.

sections.h2: What does the city require before a Lakewood rental changes hands?
sections.html:
Lakewood requires a housing license for any dwelling unit rented to another person, and the Housing and Building Department collects the fees. The city's page lists $75.00 per unit for non-owner occupied one or two family structures, $60.00 per unit for three family dwellings, $45.00 per unit for other non-owner occupied dwellings, and $200.00 per building for a vacant property license. Owners who miss the November 1 deadline pay a $25.00 late fee per unit.

Since September 1, 2019, a certificate of code compliance is required before the sale of any non-owner occupied residential rental property. The point of sale inspection covers the interior, exterior and yard before the certificate issues, and the rules sit in Lakewood Codified Ordinances sections 1173.01 and 1306.53. To schedule one, call the Division of Housing and Building at (216) 529-6270 or write to building.permits@lakewoodoh.gov.

Start this process before you sign a purchase contract. An inspector's list of repairs is far easier to handle when you know about it at the start of a sale than at the closing table.

sections.h2: How are deeds and rental registrations handled in Cuyahoga County?
sections.html:
Lakewood is in Cuyahoga County, where the Fiscal Officer's Real Estate Services office handles transfers and recording at 2079 E. Ninth Street, fourth floor, Cleveland. The office page lists weekday hours and a recording cutoff of 4:00 p.m., so plan to arrive early. Each transfer needs a DTE 100 statement of value or a DTE 100 EX exemption statement. The standard recording charge, raised on October 24, 2024 under Senate Bill 94, is $39 for the opening pair of pages plus $8 per added page.

A separate county duty falls on rental owners. Ohio Revised Code 5323.02 requires a one time filing with the Fiscal Officer, with no fee, and any change must be reported within 60 days. The county says a $50 penalty can follow each tax bill when the filing is missing, and that this filing is needed even if the city has the rental on record. A buyer of your rental will need to file, and under Revised Code 319.202 the auditor's endorsement on the conveyance flags this.

Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 requires the property disclosure form on one to four unit residential sales, with exceptions for fiduciary transfers and sales to a buyer who occupied the property for twelve months. For the conveyance fee rate that applies in Cuyahoga County, ask the Fiscal Officer before closing.

faqs.q: Does a Lakewood rental need an inspection before it can be sold?
faqs.a: Yes. Lakewood's code requires a certificate of code compliance before the sale of a non-owner occupied residential rental, and a point of sale inspection comes first. Call (216) 529-6270 to schedule it.

faqs.q: What does a Lakewood housing license cost?
faqs.a: The city lists $75.00 per unit for non-owner occupied one or two family structures, $60.00 per unit for three family dwellings, and $45.00 per unit for other non-owner occupied dwellings. Late applications after November 1 add $25.00 per unit.

faqs.q: Where do deeds for Lakewood houses get filed?
faqs.a: They go to the Cuyahoga County Fiscal Officer's Transfer and Recording office in Cleveland. A DTE 100 or DTE 100 EX form has to accompany the deed.

faqs.q: Is the disclosure form still required when a Lakewood house sells as is?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 covers sales of homes with up to four dwelling units, and calling the sale as is does not replace the form. Estate fiduciaries and several other transfers are exempt.

faqs.q: Does the buyer of my Lakewood rental have to register it with the county?
faqs.a: Yes, a new owner of residential rental property files with the Cuyahoga County Fiscal Officer under Revised Code 5323.02, even when the rental is already registered with the city. There is no filing fee, but a $50 penalty can follow each tax bill if the filing is missing.
